BDRIBS(2): Poisson model with the total time at risk

Source: vignettes/bdribs2.Rmd
bdribs2.Rmd
library(bssd)

Model

BDRIBS(2) is the modification of BDRIBS(1) examined by Duncan (2026, Section 3.2.3): the total exposure time is replaced by the total time at risk, in which the time after the first occurrence of the event is discarded. For subject \(i\) with the follow-up time \(t_i\) and the time to the first event \(s_i\) (\(s_i = \infty\) for a subject without the event), the two exposures are \[E_1 = \sum_i t_i \quad \text{(BDRIBS(1))}, \qquad E_2 = \sum_i \min(t_i, s_i) \quad \text{(BDRIBS(2))}.\] The rest of the model is that of BDRIBS(1) (vignette("bdribs1")): \[Y \sim \mathrm{Poisson}\{E_2 \delta (r k + 1) / (k + 1)\}, \quad \delta \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(\lambda_{HP} PT_{HP} / DF, PT_{HP} / DF), \quad r = \frac{p}{k (1 - p)}, \quad p \sim \mathrm{Beta}(a, b).\]

The number of subjects with the event, \(Y\), counts first events only, and a subject cannot have a first event after it. With the total exposure time, this time is still counted as exposure, so that the exposure is too large for the observed number of events. Duncan (2026, Section 3.2.3) notes that the distinction has no impact for small incidences and a noticeable impact for larger ones, and BDRIBS(1) has lower power than BDRIBS(2) at medium and high incidences (Duncan, 2026, Section 4.1).

BDRIBS(2) uses the same function as BDRIBS(1), bdribs_post(), with the total time at risk as exposure. The other arguments are described in vignette("bdribs1"). time_at_risk() computes both exposures from subject-level data.

Example

The following data are simulated with sim_blinded() with incidences of the high-incidence scenarios of Duncan (2026, Table 1): 200 subjects randomized 1:1 with uniform entry over 26 weeks, 52 weeks of follow-up, and exponential times to the event with cumulative incidences of 30% on placebo and 45% on the study drug at week 52. The blinded analysis is at week 78, when all subjects have completed follow-up.

set.seed(2026)
rate_of <- function(ip, t) -log(1 - ip) / t
d <- sim_blinded(n = 200, k = 1, accrual = 26, follow_up = 52,
                 analysis_time = 78, dist = "exponential",
                 par_p = rate_of(0.30, 52), par_d = rate_of(0.45, 52))
tar <- time_at_risk(d$follow_up, d$event, d$event_time)
tar
#>     exposure time_at_risk      n_event 
#>    10400.000     7837.746       84.000

The total time at risk is 75% of the total exposure time. The prior of \(\delta\) is based on a historical placebo group of 100 subjects followed for 52 weeks with the incidence of 30%, discounted by \(DF = 2\).

fits <- list(
  BDRIBS1 = bdribs_post(y = tar[["n_event"]], exposure = tar[["exposure"]],
                        k = 1, lambda_hp = rate_of(0.30, 52),
                        pt_hp = 100 * 52, df = 2, t_star = 52),
  BDRIBS2 = bdribs_post(y = tar[["n_event"]],
                        exposure = tar[["time_at_risk"]], k = 1,
                        lambda_hp = rate_of(0.30, 52), pt_hp = 100 * 52,
                        df = 2, t_star = 52)
)
res <- do.call(rbind, lapply(fits, summary))
res$model <- names(fits)
knitr::kable(res[, c("model", "prob", "signal", "rr_median", "ip_placebo",
                     "ip_drug", "ip_difference")], digits = 3,
             row.names = FALSE)
model prob signal rr_median ip_placebo ip_drug ip_difference
BDRIBS1 0.668 FALSE 1.241 0.311 0.359 0.048
BDRIBS2 0.948 FALSE 2.012 0.308 0.514 0.205

The last three columns are the posterior means of the cumulative incidences at week 52 and of their difference; the true values are 0.30, 0.45 and 0.15. The posterior means of the placebo incidence are 0.311 with the total exposure time and 0.308 with the total time at risk.

Operating characteristics

The folder reproduce of the installed package contains the simulations of Figures 2 to 10 of Duncan (2026) with 1,000 simulated trials per scenario. For the medium (Figure 3) and high (Figure 4) incidences, the proportions of trials with a signal (power) of the two models are

Figure Placebo Study drug N Analysis (week) Threshold BDRIBS(1) BDRIBS(2)
3 10% 10% 350 69.3 0.925 0.000 0.000
3 10% 15% 350 69.3 0.925 0.002 0.016
3 10% 20% 350 69.3 0.925 0.039 0.151
3 10% 25% 350 69.3 0.925 0.381 0.659
4 30% 30% 200 78.0 0.95 0.000 0.000
4 30% 40% 200 78.0 0.95 0.000 0.009
4 30% 45% 200 78.0 0.95 0.000 0.068
4 30% 50% 200 78.0 0.95 0.000 0.182

The incidences are at week 52. BDRIBS(1) has much lower power than BDRIBS(2), as stated by Duncan (2026, Section 4.1); the corresponding statements of the article are judged PASS (Figure 3) and PASS (Figure 4) in inst/reproduce/reproduce_Duncan2026_figures.R. The article does not report all settings of the simulations, so the published powers are not reproduced exactly; results/SUMMARY.md in the folder reproduce gives the details.

Numerical integration and comparison with MCMC

The posterior computation of BDRIBS(2) is that of BDRIBS(1) with another exposure. The numerical integration is described in vignette("bdribs1"), and the comparison with MCMC is repeated here.

The bdribs package of Mukhopadhyay et al. (2018) samples the same model by MCMC with JAGS. The script inst/validation/validate_bdribs_package.R compares bdribs_post() with bdribs::bdribs() for the settings below, in which E is the exposure given to both functions. The results in this section are read from the output of that script (validate_bdribs_package.csv in the folder validation/results of the installed package); JAGS is not run when this article is built.

B2 5 500 2 18 4000 Gamma prior (inf.type = 2) Beta(1, 1)
B3 5 500 2 18 4000 fixed (inf.type = 1) Beta(0.5, 0.5)
B4 9 540 2 33 3000 fixed (inf.type = 1) Beta(1, 1)

bdribs::bdribs() was run with 2 chains, 5,000 burn-in iterations and 100,000 iterations. The Monte Carlo standard error (SE) of each MCMC estimate uses the effective sample size of the draws (coda::effectiveSize()); for the posterior probabilities, the effective sample sizes are between 46,649 and 115,901. For the median, the table shows the MCMC proportion of draws below the posterior median computed by bssd, which should be 0.5. The column Ratio is the absolute difference divided by the SE.

In all 35 items, the bssd value is within 2.6 standard errors of the MCMC value, and 33 items are within two standard errors. The largest absolute difference in a posterior probability is 0.0036, while the SEs of the MCMC probabilities are between 0.0015 and 0.0023. Differences of this size are expected from the Monte Carlo error of MCMC alone, so the difference between the numerical integration of bssd and MCMC is negligible in practice. The validation script judges an item PASS when the difference is at most four standard errors; 35 of the 35 items are PASS.

References

Duncan, B. (2026). Robust safety monitoring and signal detection using alternatives to the standard Poisson distribution. Journal of Biopharmaceutical Statistics, 36(2), 227-244. https://doi.org/10.1080/10543406.2024.2395532

Mukhopadhyay, S., Waterhouse, B., and Hartford, A. (2018). Bayesian detection of potential risk using inference on blinded safety data. Pharmaceutical Statistics, 17(6), 823-834. https://doi.org/10.1002/pst.1898
